en: Salutations to Śrī Rādhā-Dāmodara, the wish-fulfilling tree of all intentions! O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Caitanya, along with Sanātana and Rūpa!
O Gopāla, O Raghunātha, O Lord obtained by [the people of] Vraja, protect me!
//1//2 He who is called the Delight of Nanda, the Increaser of the Joy of the Three Worlds, he who is indeed the Lord of the gopīs whose births are established as beginningless. //2//
I bow to that Kṛṣṇa, who is dark as a fresh rain-cloud, whose eyes are like lotuses, the delighter of the cowherd girls, appearing in the form of a cowherd boy. [3 (a pair)] 4
In the forest of Vṛndāvana, a certain aged living being said to his mind:
"O fool, you are dying right now; drink this secret nectar!
O heart, while drinking it, realize yourself as being united with Gokula."
And meditate upon some desired service with a variety of emotional states.
May the beloved of the cowherd women— the son of the mountain-king of the cowherds, who is auspicious for all the worlds— protect us by causing future prosperity to sprout forth.
"Aho! Bakī!"— with such words beginning with this praise, Kṛṣṇa himself, the Blessed Lord,
who had assumed the roles of father and so forth for her sake,
was praised by the virtuous as one of great fortune, and thus it was said.
"Neither Viriñca, nor Śrī, nor even Brahmā [is his equal]," so say the people.
Who on this earth, possessed of senses, would not take refuge in him?
Therefore, O brother, protector of yourself, take refuge in him with all your heart. (8–9)
O mind, honor this instruction, which is like a region of nectar; for it is a kalpa that bears the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree. (10) [A triad of verses]
The root is His birth and other pastimes; the trunk is His eternal play; the branches are the verses on His various seasonal activities; and the fruit is the state consisting of divine love. //11//
Now follows the play of the birth and other events by Mahākulaka.
He who was secretly proclaimed as the joy of Śrīnanda in the Tantras and Mantras manifested his own true form upon this earth out of some playful curiosity. (12)

He who, from the mere fact of his birth, created for himself a multitude of all supernatural powers, a herd of joyful beings, and a garden—a true abode—for those goddesses being born. //15//
He who, having filled [the vessel] with the nectar of his own sweetness and serving it, surpassed the form of Mohinī on the shore of the Ocean of Milk. 16.
That newborn infant, manifesting compassion, brought even Pūtanā to a state of purity and caused her to attain the exalted status of a nurse; he who,
with the tip of his tender foot, overturned that massive cart.
Thinking it to be an obstruction to his own moonlight, he cast it away as if he were impatient. //18//
He, by the splendor of his honored strides, warbling, smiles, and radiance, captivated even those young maidens who were the guardians of their families. //19//
Having attained his own name and the various lineages descending from Garga, he who spoke thus with his face turned toward Soma-jit showered joy upon those below, saying "Om. (20)
Having encountered Tṛṇāvarta, who was immediately setting the world to destruction,
he brought him— who was intent on universal ruin— to a state of utter confusion.
He who, sporting with pure playfulness, associates with Śrī Rāma—his own garden—and delights the children, is the son of Nanda-rāja, the lion among men. //22//
He who wore a forehead mark shining with yellow pigment and a bodice with the luster of gold was then born resting upon his mother’s lap. (23)
He who, while engaged in the play of mud, was held by her with sincere affection, created through both their joy and sorrow those who are tenderly attached and deeply pierced [by love]. (24)
He whose mind was somewhat timid, seeing his mother splashing together with him in the mud of the courtyard, quickly went to her. //25//
He who was embraced by her drank deeply from her breast with undistracted mind while she smiled; and she, bearing that smile, looked up at him as he grew well-nourished. //26//
At that time, he brought back to his mother everything she had completely forgotten, as if speaking with the bewildered glance of a young lion. (27)
Was he who was then eating clay, unnoticed by her, protected by her yoga-māyā out of compassion, or was he saved from her out of fear? //28//
He who belongs to the lineage of Śrī Rāma danced out his desires with great skill, providing the rhythmic beat and protection that bring happiness to the elders and prosperity to the wealthy. //29//
He who, even when the price was dropped from his hand, gave immeasurable fruits—fruits unobtainable by others—to the woman selling them. 30. 1. (a) *mārāmaṃ*; 2. (b) [omitted]

Even as he was pulling his calf’s tail along with Saṅkarṣaṇa,
he was mocked by his brothers’ wives as he walked away dragging it.
He who, though committing theft of cows, shone for the sake of the worthy;
and whose dispute with them was for the sake of establishing a pleasant conversation. (33)

He who, while listening to [the stories of] his own Dāmodara, approaches him with joy and bashfulness, even more so than out of affection born from his mother’s instruction or from his own childhood inclinations. //34//
He who was thoroughly possessed by playfulness did not come quickly even when repeatedly called by his mother with affection, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa, lotus-eyed one! (35)
He who, arriving at the forest-dwelling of Śrī Vṛndāvana together with his brother, caused both mothers and sisters-in-law to laugh and shine with joy. (36)
When Śrī Vṛndāvana was attained, he experienced the pastime already commenced there, forming friendship with Rāma, Dāman, and others, as well as with bees and other creatures similar to them. (37)
There too, he experienced supreme joy upon seeing Vṛndāvana, Govardhana, and the sandy banks of the Yamunā along with Śrī Rāma. //38//
He who, having reached middle youth, was going to the forest with his father, attained joy as he inquired after the names of the sacred abodes and beheld them. (39)
The son of the King of Vraja, playing as a child without shame, engaged in mutual chatter with his elder brother, grappling hand-to-hand and foot-to-foot.
And he, while tending his own calves, struck down the Dānava named Vatsaka—
who was like a crane in form— after tearing him apart, as he had previously tormented Mukta.
He who performed his own sport known as the "stealing of the ewe," and rendered the sky void by making it subject to reversal. //42//

He who, while committing that fragmentary sin, was led beyond further evil by his own light—that light of devotion which is both prior and yet more proximate—[was drawn] into the splendor of devotion. 43.
He who, having passed beyond childhood and adorned with the beauty of youth, assumed the role of a cowherd while proceeding to become the protector of the world's guardians. 44.
He who, out of compassion, restored consciousness to the inhabitants of Vraja whose senses were crushed by the *kālakūṭa* poison, by raining down the nectar of his glances. //45//
He who, by manifesting even Kāliya with the imprint of His own pair of feet, indicated "I am this" and thus gladdened other seekers who had come for refuge. //46//
He who was thus described by Śuka as the object of the love of Vraja, having spoken such words as "one whose self and friends are offered to Kṛṣṇa," and having lamented [for him]... 47.

He who, by his touch, turns poison and the venomous serpent into nectar— such a skillful one has demonstrated the principle of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument) in order to transform those who depend on him into nectar.
Having reached Bhāṇḍīra, that prince, performing a *malla-tāṇḍava* (wrestler’s dance),

Gopālī, Pālikā, Dhanyā, Viśākhā who is established in meditation, Rādhā, Anurādhā, Somābhā, Tārakā, and likewise Daśamī. //54//

Having gone to the Kāmyaka forest, he sports eternally with his companions at the lake resembling the ocean, which is like Laṅkā in its appearance and adorned with ornaments. (56)
Then, like a bee toward spring, he who was a virtuous man made his own mind flicker through youth, causing the lotus-like women to tremble.
He, whose nature is curiosity, secretly delighted those eternal beloveds of Vraja by means of his power of divine play (līlā-śakti), leading them to appear otherwise [than they truly were]. //58//
He who, while protecting the cows with Śrī Rāma, struck down the demon Dhenuka—
who was an obstacle— and thereby brought about fearlessness in heaven.
He who, having taken his cow, returned to the pen in the evening, experienced an unprecedented passion for the young maidens through their intense gazing. (60)
He who previously, out of modesty, abandoned the means of messengers, love-letters, and the like, now made the corner of his own eye serve as a brand-new messenger. (61)
Having clearly become attached to them and then quickly becoming detached from everything, he mastered the art of the flute for the sake of begging alms by means of contact with their limbs. (62)
Even though he quickly pulled them with his bamboo pole, he was unable to pull those conscious and unconscious beings out effectively,
because they remained rooted there out of shame.

He who, through the playful deception of Śrīdāman, Sudāman, Bhadrasena, Arjuna, and others, by means of his power, brought about the humiliation of that Pralamba. //65//
He who, by his strength and splendor, having rendered Pralamba— who was hanging down— deprived of life, established the fierce Navashakti in a most distant place.
He who, having sported in the forest throughout the long days of the summer heat, bestowed such joy upon his beloveds in the afternoon as they had never known before. 68.
At the sight of Govinda, the supreme bliss of the gopīs arose;
for them, a single moment in his absence had become like a hundred yugas. (69)

He who always brings about the sight of rain when the night of the rainy season has ended, having reached the autumn morning, does not steal away the vision of beloved ones. (70)
He who, having transferred his love for Śrī Govardhana into his own life, his wealth, and his very self—even toward those of his own kin—taught this same devotion to other noble souls as well. (71)
He who, bearing Śrī Govardhana, brought about the loss of pride in Indra, and who raised up his own herd of cattle— the most excellent among those dear to him— to a preeminent status.
Finding the state of being Govinda, he attained the state of delighting the universe;
for by his mutual friendship toward Śakra and all living beings, he bestowed the nature of Śambhu upon them.

He who, having brought his father from the world of the noose-bearer (Yama), restored him to life as if he were his mother’s very breath, caused the entire Vraja to lose its life when he was gone. 74.
He who dispelled the sorrow from the hearts of his own people, the inhabitants of Vraja,
caused them as well as himself to behold Goloka, the eternal realm.
He who, having taken the garments of the mind, bestowed them upon the maidens—who had never before been bound by him—has now bound them eternally within himself. (76)
He who, following Rādhikā—who was afflicted by delusion due to her own lineage—composed verse after verse beginning with "The Pulinda women were full [of longing]," and so forth. (77)
He, the bestower of joy, at the end of summer, out of the abundance of his love and with great delight, summoned all his foremost friends in this sequence. (78)
O Stokakṛṣṇa, O Aṃśu, O Śrīdāman, Subala, and Arjuna;
O Viśāla, Vṛṣabha, Ojasvin, Devaprastha, and Varūthapa! //79//
Having thus addressed them again with words that were playful yet truthful,
he spoke of the supreme destination for the stationary beings residing in Vṛndāvana.

Manifesting his hunger through his friends, he fashioned a request for alms-food. //81//
He who was observed by them while playing with his friends in that auspicious Ashoka grove, and who was described by them as "the Dark One" (Shyama), and so forth— [82]—
He who always sought the pleasure of amusement, having appointed the one named Madhumangala as his counselor for jests, delighted his friends with food. //83//
Like a rain-cloud to the *cātaka* birds that depend on him for their very lives, he established a state of identity with the beautiful-browed women of Vraja by means of his own life. 84.

He who, having observed perfection in the training of the flute after only a short time, immediately and naturally considered himself to have been quickly perfected by it through his beloved. 86.
He who, under the pretext of renunciation, spoke jests toward his beloveds,
found happiness by receiving playful retorts from the group of women who delighted in such jesting.

that which begins with "even the female deer" (*eṇapatnī*) is considered there to be nectar for the ears. 91.
He who, having become distracted by their lamentations beginning with "Who will conquer them?", appeared before them in this manner, as described by the wise. (92)
The saffron from whose breasts rested upon their excellent garments and seats shone like the moonlight upon a sandy bank ruled by the king of stars. //93//

O King, it was well known that the Blessed One shone there with supreme splendor, just as the dark-complexioned one [Kṛṣṇa] does when accompanied by golden-hued women. 95.

He who, bestowing life upon all living beings, approached his father crawling on his hands and knees, and thereby warded off the sage’s curse by touching the serpent. //99//
He who, out of compassion, led the great serpent Kūṭadanta—who was of evil vision—to a state of right vision; and who did not even commit a cruel act against Kaṅkāla. (100)
I consider that festival of the Yakṣa, Dhūrvaṇa, which was formerly established by him, to be like the Antaryāma sacrifice among such rustic festivals. (101)
He who, engaged in sports beginning at dawn, even while shining amidst them, was daily celebrated by those women with a collection of pairs of verses. (102)
He who, on Śrī Govardhana, increases the desire to expand the *rāsa* dance, and having united with the assembly of his beloveds, delights in the arena of playful competition; //103//
Having heard from the cow-pen a harsh cry uttered by an omen of misfortune, he gathered there, restrained it, struck it down, and attained joy. (104)
Again, proceeding swiftly toward the mountain with his companions who were full of graceful gestures, he caused the *rāsa* dance to flourish and illuminated everything. 105.

He who, with a gaze of affectionate smiles, with speech like nectar,
with faultless conduct, and with a self that is the very abode of splendor— //109//

He whose own various qualities were sufficient to abandon all others, yet whom they could not abandon—let alone those heroes of love in Vraja; even the mere mention of him from afar is enough. (115)
One who has always attained the qualities described at the beginning of the Dharma in the first book of the *Pṛthvī* [Mahākāvya] should likewise be praised here as well; let him be heeded. (116)
The root of bliss that bestows all joy, likewise the series of its qualities; by virtue of the greatness of all its festivals, it is superior in every respect and is the Lord. //117//
Always partaking in growth, it is the wealth of the ground for the propitiation of all;
it bestows the merit of the excellence of one's own nature and form, and grants the bliss of action. //118//
His vision possesses the splendor of the beautiful radiance of a shower of nectar;
his voice, which brings joy to the ears, flows like a stream from every direction. //119//
The fragrance of his breath, which brings forth a heavy scent that causes even horses to neigh, possesses a beauty created by the nectar of his tongue as it touches his lower lip. 120.
By touching that which touches itself, he removes the sins of universal suffering;
he is the abode of purity for the world, and he is praised by the recollection of his name. //121//

Viṣṇu, the conqueror of Ramā, possesses a body that illuminates the infinite light of existence, consciousness, and bliss; his form is a mass of rays that outshines even the brilliance of fine garments. 122.

He who bears the splendor that refines the world, who is adorned by ornaments that themselves serve as ornaments, and whose form possesses qualities that swiftly pervade all according to his will. //123//
The glory of his own status, marked by the conch, discus, and other signs, is impossible to conceal. //124//
With a series of ever-delightful powers that never cease even to conquer his own self, he possesses the essence of the mind of a youth and is the thief who utterly deludes the entire world. (125)
He has conquered the arts of graceful movement, laughter, and dance through his playful charm;
his form is free from worldly transformations, yet it is animated by the transformation of radiant love. //126//
Though ancient, he is thus determined to be ever-new; though his body is not new, the glorious one always possesses a body that is as if newly formed.
With a radiant mind, he was well-disposed toward making the minds of all joyful;
he was the intellect that created the intelligence of all beings and the one who brought about the perfection of even the perfections themselves.
He was the instructor of hundreds of thousands of skills and was distinguished by his own exceptional dexterity. //129//
Out of gratitude, he turned a drop of trivial assistance into an ocean.

and by means of his fame and majesty, he brought relief to the suffering world. //135//

He who brings bliss to the devotion of his devotees, who is won over by the stability of their love, and who experiences wonder at the limits of his own manifestations through their various forms, qualities, and pastimes. //141//
Through the consecration of affection, he is honored with the vast sovereignty of all;
he is a constant cloud raining down the nectar of love everywhere. //142//

he is worshipped by the beloved of Viṣṇu (Lakṣmī), who yearns for the fortune of his own circle of dear consorts.

Her complexion shone like the playful flash of lightning from a beloved cloud; she was adorned with garments praised for their excellent colors, which were as dear to her as her own skin;

Her own form attains the state of being a metaphor for itself, her mass of limbs exquisitely adorned with perfect proportions; her glory is marked by innate and extraordinary characteristics, spreading auspiciousness in every direction. (24)

Even her foot, with its luster like that of the moon-lotus, conquers other limbs by means of the brilliance of its own nails; let every other part of her body be something else, for it has captured the heart of the lovely one with its ever-fresh radiance.

She is an entrance into the most delicate of delicate blossoms; she is the glory that creates the fragrance of fragrances throughout the three worlds; and she has attained renown through a style of description overflowing with a manner of expression that is truthful, measured, sweet, dear, and purposeful. //26//
Possessing a most profound intellect and all branches of knowledge, her mind was deeply bowed by the embrace of every art;

The Earth, who is the abode of supreme devotion toward the multitude of her gurus and the object of their compassion, is ever weighed against him alone—her own beloved—who possesses all virtues such as gentleness and mercy; she is consecrated by the nectar of the heartfelt happiness of both the stationary and moving beings. Even though Hari is skilled in all the arts, he finds satisfaction in only a small portion of them;
even though those in the assembly have mastered the arts, they take delight merely in beholding the face of Hari.
Thinking, "Alas, he never attends the entire assembly of poetry, drama,
and the like," the Lord of Vraja, with the consent of his wife who was aware of their separation night after night, performed that which was most dear to her.
At one time at night the king desired poetry, at another the art of drama, and yet another painting;
though all these appeared separately, Hari alone manifested them all before him. (306)
When the watch of the night had thus passed with many wonders, all the people, accompanied by Hari’s army, beheld the king of the Vrajas risen and stood respectfully awaiting his command. (307)
When his father, the conqueror of Mura, was unable to say anything and his throat was choked with tears,
the elder teachers, having informed the two of them, performed the mental rites for the sake of the funeral preparation.
Having caused his father to bow before the others according to their merit, and having made them bear humility and modesty, Kṛṣṇa,
accompanied by his brothers, followed his two mothers for a long time, enjoying the affectionate care they bestowed upon him as was fitting.
Then, perceiving the consent granted by his mother and her husband, bowing with a humble gaze,
and having followed and saluted the wielder of the plow (Balarāma), he, having attained the status of a bridegroom for the first time, returned to his own dwelling.

4. (a) Describing Kṛṣṇa as "the one who has drunk nectar" (*amṛtāśu*), that group—Rādhikā and her companions—beholding even Kṛṣṇa at the threshold of the house, descended very quickly and practiced the concealment of their own identities. //311//
In this matter, another opinion is held: "May he always follow after all lovely women; let it be thus.
But, O heart, consider this: you must remember everywhere the beautiful deeds of Rādhā and Hari. 312.
Then, Hari, beautifully attired, suddenly approached with Vṛṣabhānu, Rādhikā, and the others;
he was like a fresh rain cloud accompanied by streaks of lightning, for their vision became as if composed of a shower of nectar. //313//

Is this a bower here, possessing the beauty of a creeper-branch with its jewel-like clusters of blossoms and sharing in their fragrance; or is it a dwelling? And what here is the flower, or what is the silken garment?
This couple that lies upon it is the bed. //314//
Thus ends the eternal pastimes. //2//
Salutations to Śrī Gopāla.
That [reality] consisting of birth and so forth, and that eternal pastime, as declared by the Vedas,
exist in a mutual relationship of prior and subsequent, like the continuous flow from seed to tree.
Now, [I shall describe] the eternal play of all seasons occurring within;

therefore, perform in your heart the praise of the Son of the Cowherd, obtained from the *Gautama-tantra*, which is diverse according to many kinds of traditional scriptures and which manifests His auspicious deeds through the devotion of His own devotees. (1)

In his birth during the spring season, in childhood, in youth, and in the possession of old age, the arts beginning with the passion of spring shone forth for the beloved and his beloved, and then subsided. //2//

Therefore, this distinct description according to each of the six seasons is intended; for indeed, Hari, performing his playful movements, wanderings, and activities here, described them at various times as follows: (3)
First, O mind, hear here the words that the captivating Rādhā spoke to her Lord one night; then,
consider Hari’s words to her in return.
Its giver is peaceful within, like nectar. //4//
“Ha! Ha! You wander through the forest of the forest, a parched wasteland scorched by the summer heat, your body emaciated and harsh.
O Slayer of Mura, I do not know how you will protect people who are themselves worn out by the very thought of you!”
Having considered what was thus spoken, Kṛṣṇa, with a smiling face, said this himself to Rādhā:
"Understand this, O mind; this wealth of yours shall become the locus for many fluctuations. (6)
“Ha! Ha! O fair-faced one, this is not something else to be inferred; even within the season of austerity, there is a wondrousness therein.
For in one place he gives experience like spring, in another like the rainy season, and in yet another, he himself [gives it] like autumn. //7//
In this forest, which is here incomparable, even this summer season shines as if it were sweet;
for the summer itself, though devoid of water, has become like the glory of the rainy season, possessing the splendor of mountain torrents. (8)
Here, Vṛndā adorns the entire forest all around with her equals among the immortals, so that day after day I may enjoy it together with you and even with your companions. (9)

May the exceedingly sweet water of the fresh coconut and the juice of the palm fruit, which resembles it, along with its kernel—offered here by Vṛndā to me who am thirsty and accompanied by my friends—grant me satisfaction. (10)
Together with my friends, I prepare a feast of the juices of the panasa, sahakāra, and gostanī fruits; yet it is strange that your lip-honey should take me there instead.
O fair-browed one, by its very density, it causes you to remember yourself.
"Now we too shall consider that site for the monastery as yours, if it is your desire."
With a slight margin [of time], Hari set out quickly for her, as indicated by the signs of the bull, the sound of the lion, and so forth. //12//
First he went to a particular forest region filled with spring, and then to another place; weighing them against one another in his experience, he spoke these words with much humor.
During the day, O fair-browed one, having beheld that excellent river before us, we would all sit together;
after each of us had drunk from our own white vessels, we would enjoy ourselves here with our friends. 14.
O moon-faced one, in this month of Śuci, at midday, within the interior of a mountain resembling a palace, its slopes surrounded by a multitude of waterfalls, I shall joyfully lie down with you. (15)

Within the interior of Vraja, amidst clusters of groves that serve as abodes for moonstones and whose depths possess high banks formed by the daughters of the Sun, I shall joyfully take refuge with you in secret during the day. 16.
"Let us go here by the current of this river and bring our pastime to a state of joyful bliss," he said as he moved along,
holding the arms of the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan while accompanied by his other friends.
Moving ever closer to the river and gradually leaving behind only the dry ground,
he reached the midst of the pair of kingdoms belonging to the kings Tapana and Madhu.
O moon-faced one, behold your own self here as if it has departed. //18//
Here, even though the lotus groves are withered by the heat, how many lotuses still remain?
Therefore, having entered this river, let us both gather them and bind them beautifully. (19)
“Wandering here and there repeatedly, searching for the flow of nectar in the river, the bees milk the lotus like a breast of the lotus-plant for their ever-new offspring. (20)
Thus, having devised this pretext of being surrounded by the forest, he led the beautiful maidens of Vraja into the river;
there, under the guise of gathering lotuses, he made them laugh at his own will in various places.
“Oh, this lotus has been obtained by me, while yours is blue, though it is renowned for its golden luster!”— thus,
under various pretexts, they went together with the Unconquered One to the heart of the monastery.
Then, wondering whether it was a lotus upon his chest or perhaps the hand of Hari,
the young women of Vraja attained a state of horripilation and soft sighs as they gazed with apprehension.
Then, as the Lord of the Mura-demons smiled there with his sidelong glances, they discharged water that had the appearance of weapons;
yet he rendered that [water] into them, though by him their disappearance was brought about for him.
Hari, the conqueror of hundreds of thousands of asuras, was himself desired to be conquered by these women;
that he obtained victory here is not surprising, but that he was then defeated is truly most wonderful in this matter. //25//

"Even though he was scattered by the sprinkling of water, even that enemy of sin did not suffer defeat," said Vārṣabhānavī, knitting her brows; and thus, in that moment, she became as if a painting. (26)

Then, assuming an air of triumph born from their playfulness toward all the women, the deer-eyed maidens quickly seized Hari; yet, through the artifice of laughter and reproach, they made him pay attention once more to them. 27.
When the lord of her life had become attentive,
the daughter of the bull-bannered god (Pārvatī) quickly went to the bank to draw him toward her; there, even the name "Kṛṣṇa," bound by passion, attained the state of being followed.

Then the maidservants quickly and very gently wiped the limbs of Murāri, the daughter of the bull-voiced one (Pārvatī), and those girls of their own age with a cloth, and they dressed them in excellent garments. //29//
Then Vṛṣabhānu’s daughter herself, lightly applying to her beloved’s limbs the powder of musk and saffron, removed the coldness from within and without, yet brought back a coldness once more. //30//
Then the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu adorned her beloved with a tilaka of exquisite saffron, while he, appearing in his most graceful attire, adorned her exceedingly with his own splendor.
The female friend placed betel rolls made from *kramuka* nut and *śita-karañja* leaves into the mouths of Hari and Rādhā;
she also placed them within the mouths of the two of them for the sake of spreading joy among the circle of their friends. 32.
Then the lotus-pools, together with their beloveds— the lovely women— desiring to go to their dwellings with graceful playfulness,
shone forth in every way with their entire sport, their beautiful eyes surpassing the petals of the lotuses.
In some places, they sported with Hari upon the lotus-thicket, laughing heartily;
yet they did not realize that here, by him alone, all the worlds have been eternally conquered. (34)
Thus, all of them together engaged in various kinds of play with him until the end of the game;
thereafter, they entered the pavilion situated in the excellent garden and were absorbed in its splendor.

This jeweled palace has transcended the enclosure of worldly existence; it is the midst of a row of excellent lakes and lotuses, a beautiful bed where one rests upon a pillow meeting a downy mattress as delicate as exquisite flowers. (36)
With his limbs refreshed by objects such as a ladle, a palm-leaf fan, and a golden water-pot placed nearby,
Hari, radiant with the glow of his smile, entered most swiftly, sat upon the couch, and reclined there.
Then the daughter of the Sun herself attended upon him, who held a flower-whisk,
while he— casting sidelong glances and full of guile and deceit— led her to the bed. (38) [Couplet]
She too, for that very reason, assumed a state of feigned lethargy out of the pretense of exhaustion;
thereafter, her companions shared in the pleasure of those two as they enjoyed betel-leaf with camphor.
Thereupon, having inferred from that [gesture] her desire for a private meeting with him, her friends departed;
however, one of them remained for a moment and performed a gentle caress for the two of them.

This sleep of the one free from duality has also departed; for, having devised a stratagem, she abandoned the closing of her pair of eyes—which was itself a stratagem—and opened her own desire consisting of love. (41)
Thus, when the summer had passed away through various kinds of diversions, the splendor of the rainy season arrived;
the body of Hari’s consort attained its beauty through the grace of the lightning-crests encircling the clouds. 42.
Cultivating a desire to describe her splendor night after night, the son of the Lord of Vraja went forth;
and the assembly of her companions, including the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu who was bearing this [desire], also rejoiced as they rose up. 43.

Thus, at the clear dawn of the rainy season, eating the milk-rice prepared for my mother—spiced with pepper, warm, and served in small portions—I enjoy happiness, looking upon the face of Anurāmā. (44)
My birthday will arrive here in the month of Bhādra, and along with it, O dear one, the welfare of the people of Vraja;
for both of these, gladdening the worlds, will be celebrated with great joy on the festival day of Purata. (45) 1.

Now, having ascended the very peak of the house-roof, behold this cow-pen dwelling even at night;
through the abundance of light from the shimmering flashes of lightning, it shines repeatedly as if it were day. //46//

O friend, the beauty of the forest now approaches me, as if it has become my own: in the sky it possesses the splendor of a mass of clouds and lightning, and upon the earth it has the shimmering luster of green indragopaka insects. 47.

In this place, which resembles the back of a tortoise, with its center filled with jewels that serve as pathways for the movement of eyes, and where fresh grass has spread and grown, I shall provide protection for the white elephants. 48.

On the summit of the best of mountains, having obtained a view of the cows from my jeweled palace with its surrounding walls cast aside, I pass my time happily with my friends, engaging in various games such as *śatarañja* and other chief diversions. //49//
While water flows from the clouds, he tastes the fruits along with their stalks within the hollows of the trees;
sitting upon a stone seat by the water, he eats well-prepared food accompanied by curds, distributed among his friends.
Sometimes, calling out "Cows! upon some mountain peak and settling there with joy while watching them, I am to be constantly beheld by you here and there as I stand upon the roof-ridge. (51)
[In this season] here blows a wind fragrant with the scent of *kadamba*, *nīpa*, and *ketaka* flowers, variegated by swarms of bees;
it carries away the distinctness of our experience, as we both perceive only a faint trace of your fragrance. //52//

O blessed lady, if you are completely overcome with horripilation upon seeing Kṛṣṇa’s golden garment, you will then attain a resemblance to the earth bearing sprouts that grow when dark clouds and lightning appear. 53.
In this rainy season, the swans and other birds produce echoes;
and those clouds, which clearly and incessantly create for one another a sound that is well-developed and profound, repeatedly cause them to hear it there.
Following the cloud, those known as the Plava, Śikhi, and Cātaka—respectively the youngest, the middle, and the chief—have taken refuge;
they rejoice solely in it according to the rule of degrees of intensity, while the other, however, has its very life dependent on that alone. (55)
"Even I, beholding this, indeed reflect upon my own devotees who have no other [deity];
and thereafter, this assembly of yours has entered my heart as the supreme. (56)
While Hari was speaking thus, a rain fell, scattering fine droplets; then the chief [attendant] set up a tent for the two of them, and around the bed, they placed a dwelling covered with cloth.
Outside, there was the roar of thick thunder accompanied by rain; inside the house, on a most excellent couch, it was but slightly cool.
Following that, this couple was dressed in fine garments—O mind, recollect this pair, white and black. (58)
Thus, as the rainy season passed away in various playful delights, autumn arrived;
and clearly perceiving that it had come just as before, Murajit spoke to her in due course during the night, as he had done previously.

Day after day, at sunrise and at the onset of autumn, having partaken with my friends of the milk and prepared food provided by my own mother, and having discerned you as one who has come from the forest through association with cows, I speak to you. (60)
Carrying experience and possessing a transparent nature, the Earth has emulated you in her own being;
for toward me, who am worthy of being supported by her in a manner befitting that, you, O fair-browed one, are indeed such as she.

When the flash of lightning vanished from the cloud, alas, my pride departed; likewise, when the cloud passed away, I repeatedly recalled the ancient likeness between that cloud and my own state at the time of your departure.
If I were to perceive, even in a small measure, the beauty of the *khañjana* bird, the swan, and the lotus along the banks of the water—[then I might find solace].
O fair-limbed one, having reflected upon your arrival, alas, I fall into delusion through the state of my wandering confusion. //63//
"Thinking, 'She desires the beauty of the eyes of Acyuta’s beloved, who is my teacher in the art of amorous play,' the great swarm of fish indeed makes the tossed lotus-stalks dance."
When, observing the water’s clarity through its lack of agitation and contemplating for a moment its inner nature, I behold my own reflection here and recall the comparison with your mind. (65)
Beholding each fresh sandbank and setting aside each step that led toward it, I placed one reason in my mind and another in my speech; you alone know this. (66)

Having gathered flowers constantly along every path and fashioned a bow and other implements made of blossoms, we have reached this bank of sand; there, let us offer an oblation to the one whose arrows are flowers.

Having fashioned a small lily bud with a slender stalk as a masterpiece rivaling autumn itself, we shall also firmly construct a bow from the leaves of the fresh *ketaka* tree, made strong by joining three or four together. 68.
Thus Hari, accompanied by his beloved and performing various sports, fashioned a bed of flowers;
laughing at those with broad bodies and uneven foliage, he made them appear slender like delicate creepers. //69//

Then he beheld a sandbank that mirrored the moon, and likewise the moon mirroring that sandbank; entering into it out of the power of the essence of curiosity, he rejoiced, perceiving himself as if drenched in nectar.
Then the circle of friends said to Mukunda, "Where indeed is the flower-arrowed god whom we should worship?
Hari replied, "I am he himself in person; know that my own worship is his."
"If the host of her friends has no power at all over me, a mere mortal,
then endure my flower-arrows directly!"— as he contemplated this, that host trembled.

Then, speaking with the voice of a bull, he said: "O Murāri, you alone have achieved victory here in this earthly battle, while discharging millions of weapons from the enemy forces; behold this! (73)
Then, as he scattered those countless flower-arrows all around him,
he shattered those arrows with his own flower-arrows, or rather, he pierced their bodices.
Then the multitude of Hari’s beloveds, wearing smiles, spoke to Hari, who was radiant with the glow of victory:
“We are young women here; therefore, point out a pleasure grove that is already familiar to us.”
Then Hari, smiling, said: "You are exceedingly proficient in the Bharata doctrine;
therefore, follow it, so that a gradation may arise among you in singing, instrumental music, and dancing. (76)
Like a liquid flowing from the throat of Hari, that [song] became the very limit of the delight for Śilāditya and the women of Hari’s court;
yet Hari remained somehow steadfast, while they were not so composed because of his singing. (77)
Then, having gathered together, he performed a dance with his own women, yet he did not attain equality with them;
they said to him, "We are not the Sandīpani."
How indeed shall we know that we have obtained a teacher?
//78// 1. (a) When it exists; 2.
(a) We have perceived [it].
Hari performed a dance presented by Taṇḍu, and by this he captivated their hearts;
here they exclaimed, "We are not even equal to a lotus, since we have been taught even this. (79)

Then, through their mutual mingling, those women performed a dance of amorous passion with that beloved; by means of the exquisite sweetness of their playful charms, the celestial nymphs were repeatedly and utterly enchanted. (80)
Then Hari performed a marvel here as well; by the splendor of his speed, he vanished so completely that all the women, upon looking, thought him to have clung to their very sides at every moment. 81.

Having experienced fatigue from practicing such amorous sports as these, they have finally settled down, refreshed by the desired services provided to them: fans, water for drinking, unguents, betel-leaf rolls, and so forth. (82)

Then, having attained profound peace at the end of the night, these women with eyes like those of a golden deer, joyfully taking pleasure in their wanderings through the forest, returned to their own jewel-like palace in the garden. //83//
Then Murāri, having obtained a soft bed known as Ādhika that provided exquisite comfort,
lay down in such a way that, although it was but a single body, it did not appear as two separate bodies.
Then, on the festival of the mountain-like lord (Śiva), during the holiday when his sisters had come home, in the month of Kārttika,
which was filled with auspiciousness and manifold splendor—
Thereafter, the eloquent mouth brings about happiness. //85//
Then, when the autumn season— the beauty of the year consisting of gentle and mild coolness— had arrived,
Hari spoke to his beloved regarding the pleasures of food, clothing, sporting in the forest and on the mountains, and the comforts of the bed.
The food was prepared with milk from a cow whose calf had been recently weaned and with grains of fragrant, fresh śāli rice;
it was overflowing on all sides with a powerful, sweet aroma and was garnished with peeled bark, seeds, and oranges. //87//

O fair-limbed one, at dawn, this variety of cakes made from flour cooked in abundant ghee—delightful with its broad, bowl-shaped *maṇḍakas*, seasoned with sliced fresh ginger, and offered by my own mother—tastes truly sweet to me. (88)
[In a pair of verses:

Thereafter, my mother gives me a garment filled with the powders of musk and saffron; wearing that day after day, I go out with Rāma along the streets with my friends and experience exceeding joy. (89)
O lotus-eyed one, even that which was perceived here as having various beginnings and middles during the day becomes, with care, like a mustard-vegetable cooked inside ghee while still moist. (90)

Day after day, we enjoy the pleasure of dalliance with our friends in the act of singing the warbling of female harītakas, which possesses a luster like that of the sun and is as bright as the skin of a cow, a bodice, and other such garments. //91//

We wander day after day through the forest regions, which are crimson with the luster of ripe jambu, nāgaraṅga, and kramuka fruits, and where all the trees are made to rejoice by the blossoms of the kaṭiñjara and other species that shimmer with smiles. //92//
O restless friend, let us gaze upon this forest while there is but a trace of frost in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
for on the following day, when it is intensely cold, wandering outside would not be appropriate. (93)

Thus, at the word of Hari, having followed him into the forest and then rested in that delightful place, they returned to the palace of the women, filled with joy, having gathered appropriate fruits and flowers. (94) 1. (a) Oparvatayā; 2. (a) [Fragmentary]
(b) On a winter night; 4. (a) "Distortion" refers to a bed made comfortable with very soft cotton mattresses, and a pair of eyes that are pleasing to behold.
The one known as Madhuripu and the daughter of Vṛṣabhānu experienced neither difference in body nor in mind. //95//

Then, in the portion of days occupied by the Sun from the sign of Sagittarius up to the end of Pisces, divided [by twelve], the Enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu) spoke to her, as before, regarding her own splendor of grace born of the bull and the sun. 96.

Various savory cakes seasoned with ghee, curd, kṛsara, ginger, and other ingredients, along with various kinds of sweets, were placed by my mother into me at sunrise every day; these bring me great happiness. (97)

Then, delighting myself, I enjoy the joy of eating various kinds of soft flour-cakes, cooked with milk and steam, filled with my favorite fillings, and sent to me day after day in portions exactly suited to my size. 98.

With a chest covered by two fine cotton garments as delicate as the softness of saffron and a bodice, I seek refuge near the cow-pen on the ground that provides the comfort of heat without the need for a fan. 99.

In this cool season, when all living beings are silent and the cuckoos have become bold in their speech, someone here surely said, "No [one else]," O friend; thus was laughter accompanied by compassion. 100.
Even when a cold, cloudy day has arisen, the white ones move about happily, free from measurement;
hear, O friend, that final and singular remedy of mine, born of the flute, which is the hymn of the Wind-god. //101//
Beholding the winter devoid of other flowers, I wear this variegated garland made here of *kunda* blossoms;
for that which serves as one's livelihood in times of adversity shines with increasing respect at every step.
Here, others censured the collection of days that had passed swiftly,
because they held it beyond the scope of their deliberation,
due to the increase of the nights resulting from your approach.
But I desire for him a long life. //103//

Now the spring season will arrive, making the multitude of forests blossom; behold its power, for even before it has fully spread, the assembly of Hari’s and Hara’s wives has already blossomed of its own accord! (104)

Then, having first properly arranged the food and other necessities for that day, Kṛṣṇacandra would listen at night to the incomparable account of the forest life of the daughter of the Sun (Savitṛ), as it had occurred day by day. //105//

Listen to this wonder seen today in the forest: even though he is a mendicant who forcibly wears a garland of flowers, the bees on that *puṇḍraka* flower—which is not born from honey—constantly carry out a threat with their humming. (106)
"Why does this Mādhavī creeper, known by that name among the people, bloom so profusely out of intoxication? Alas, alas! It is not from the spring (madhu) that she blooms thus."
And indeed, the saptalā and other plants produced flowers. //107//

The row of Bakula, Sahakāra, and Ketakī trees, along with Karuṇa, Kiṃśuka, and Nāgakeśara, shone most brilliantly as the excellent bees and cuckoos, having beheld them, flew about and became attached to their splendor. 108.
This host of winds, known by the name "Malayaja-marut" (the breeze from the sandalwood mountain), having entered my poetic composition,
moves very slowly here like a suitor who has purchased a bride highly praised for her excellence over other women.
Thus, describing the excellence of the spring season, the Enemy of Madhu (Kṛṣṇa) praised her, while under the guise of describing the conduct of other beloved women,
he was actually revealing the character of other heroines.

This swarm of bees and cuckoos maintains its state as the heroine and its own nature only so long as there is companionship with beloveds; but when the time of others arrives, they assume the state of autumn and the nature of a thunderbolt toward those same beloveds. (111)

O moon-faced one, O lady with limbs as dear as a lover's, surely other women, overcome by despair due to separation from their beloveds—or perhaps tormented by bees and cuckoos—are now wandering about, driven by the power of love. 112.
Unable to endure one another's mutual glances, these co-wives approached their beloved secretly on the road;
though they tried to drive him away from every direction and sub-direction as he shimmered nearby, they could not do so—for where else could they have found him? 113.
In a certain bower-dwelling, those women who had prepared their beds for the night, having restrained their steps,
were overcome with pride upon failing to find their beloveds.
For fortunate women, whose wealth is their honor, are like a face. //114//
Moreover, those other women, having prepared their garments and repeatedly attained the power of a wish-fulfilling tree through their thoughts,
remained awake there upon finding their beloveds.
Like a fold, it experiences pleasure, yet there is no division here. //115//
Was there not even a single woman whose hopes were shattered by her most beloved, such that she became a *kalahāntaritā* (one separated by a quarrel)?
For this alone is indeed appropriate, since how else could one who is most beloved act? (116)
There is no object whatsoever capable of leading you to a state of separation from me;
nor does even the triad of waking and other states have the power here to deprive a person of consciousness. (117)
O fair-faced one, let us go this very night with haste to that cluster of bowers along with our many companions;
for here, under the light of the moon, there are blooming flowers such as the night-lotus and the mudgara.
Then Vidhu, accompanied by his beloved and his friends, went playfully to a flower garden;
yet clearly, another moon appeared there with its swarm [of bees], acting as a garland of homage over him. 119.
Then, the daughter of Vṛṣākapi, radiant with beauty, approached Hari in the stainless Kusumavana grove, accompanied by her circle of dear companions such as Sukhasarā, Lalitā, and Viśākhikā. 120.
O slender one, placing clusters of *sukusuma* flowers upon yourself and likewise applying them to him,
you make both of you radiant with joy through those acts of devotion and the flowing streams of your tears.

"Is it not so that our Queen, desiring the mass of flowers above, herself bestowing various favors upon you, swiftly carries out your command?"—thus she spoke with words accompanied by smiles and sidelong glances. (122)
As she repeatedly placed this Rāmā upon his heart with her two arms as if by force, for the sake of the upward-pointing flower,
she seemed to fulfill his desire while weeping.
By those spreading a laughter full of every musical note. //123//

She gazed at the peak of that mass of beautiful flowers, observing it as if it were herself; meanwhile, with various modes of speech, she spoke both falsehoods and truths through the diversity of her smiles. //124//

While he was quickly fashioning a cluster [of flowers] consisting of floral arrangements and simultaneously creating it separately, she—by means of a multitude of words containing desire—extended both praise and blame toward those two [objects]. //126// 1.

While he was praising the ornaments he himself had composed for it, the women, praising each of those very ornaments he had fashioned, laughed at him, saying, "In this world, such is the nature of things: one develops a sense of greatness born from one's own creation. (127)

And here, O mind, behold the wonder: though he has brought her qualities, actions, limbs, and very being under his control, the husband carries out the command of his submissive wife; yet he performs that work for her even without her being present. 127.

Here, Hari, generating the passion of spring, and the multitude of Hari’s women, exceedingly flourishing, having mastered the world through their mastery of the rhythms (*tāla*) of dance consisting of dramatic representation, brought the entire universe under their own control. 128.
Thus, as the night reached its conclusion through various sports, that lord of serpents,
dwelling within a grove of fragrant flowering trees, obtained a moment’s rest with his beloved.

On the couch at the excellent jeweled courtyard, attended with great care by the playful breeze of flowers, he—whose swarm of bees was being driven away by his supreme friends—enjoyed happiness in blissful ease. //130//
Thus ends the play of all seasons. //3//
Then, as the fruit was being realized,
He played with His own circle of companions— which brought joy to the faces of His parents— within the treasury of His own love in Ghoṣa;
yet seeing that [place] had become exceedingly terrifying due to those sent by Kaṃsa, He repeatedly struck them down.
Not seeing them, He went to the city of Madhupurī to slay them; having gone there with His entourage and slain that Ghoṣa, He returned. I always worship Him who bestows incomparable bliss. //1//

Rādhā and the other beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, having themselves undergone an incarnation like Kṛṣṇa’s through the power of his divine play (līlā-śakti), forgot their eternal state; yet, perceiving Kṛṣṇa as something other than themselves,
they remained devoted to the bliss of taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa with an unmanifested passion, and ultimately [attained] Kṛṣṇa alone.
Clearly they have gone to their own beloved; we, with our inner selves submerged in an ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss, [remain here]. //2//

O, what happiness! The enemy of Mura, having slain the wicked Kaṃsa and others who were most dear to the assembly of his cruel army, has thoroughly brought peace to the people, including his own father, whose minds had been tormented by them. Furthermore, he has removed the sufferings of those who outwardly proclaim him to be their beloved lord.
Cutting through the pain of separation from this or that, he shines forth in the assembly of those who have transcended worldly vision. //3//
In the morning, having received permission from his father and others, he who brings the joy of food from his mother’s hand,
being devoted to Śrī Rāma and the rest, joyfully protects hundreds of herds of cows;
at twilight, he goes to the houses of the cowherds and cowherdesses to grant them happiness, and throughout the night, he remains full of passion for them.
May that moon-like Kṛṣṇa, whose divine pastimes shine forth in various ways, forever cause your mind to blossom. //4//
Displaying his own life-story from birth onwards— primarily through visual means— by employing the arts of poetry, dramatic performance, and painting,
both in public assemblies and in private; and recounting the history of his beloved’s first love and so forth,
according to the specific nature of each group present, he, the victorious one, makes every festival a source of universal delight.
May the son of Nanda, who delights in sporting with splendors that shine ever more brightly, rejoice! //5//

He who is the kinsman of the ranks of bound souls (*paśu*) through his practice of begging even from Śrī; who was born as the son of Yaśodā and Nanda; who is the friend of Subala and others, and moreover the beloved of Rādhā and her companions;
he, known by the name Śrī-Gopāla, protecting the glory of the lineage of Surabhi, performs divine pastimes.
May that most graceful gait [of Kṛṣṇa], which is ever present during the nighttime pastimes such as the Rāsa dance, be our constant refuge. //6//

O moon of glorious Vṛndāvana, the bees, birds, and deer; the rows of people, the twice-born, the servants, the calves, and the groups beginning with companions, Haladhara, father, and mother; and among them, the beloveds headed by Rādhā with her excellent glances—such is the multitude, just as it is in the higher realms.
Alas, when shall we see such intoxication, thirsting for the light of that [form], day after day? //7// (Note:

The flood-crosser: 3. (a) He constantly speaks, meditates on his state of being far away, and perceives the subtle expansion that exists within the vastness; yet, when engaged in play, he gazes upon [the beloved] standing in the midst of her friends.
The couple named Rādhā and Mādhava have transcended immeasurable obstacles;
if they remain here as a divine pair, what need is there to mention if they have attained privacy? //8//
Having repeatedly overcome the separation from the pair of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, the couple, now enjoying their wedded state,
gaze at each other’s face in private with tears; amidst the intervals of one partner falling asleep, the other wipes away the moisture from the eye-sockets while pressing the tip of the nose upward.
He kisses the pair of cheeks with his heart; he melts away into bliss, meeting it within the heart. //9//

Always intoxicated by the mass of the nectar-like fragrance of their mutual affection, they dance with pure festivals of playful glances that shine with fair and dark luster, their souls anointed with the mastery of every art of enchantment.
May my mind be completely overwhelmed by the immeasurable sweetness of Rādhā and Mādhava. //10//
Thus is the accomplishment of the fruit.

"O virtuous lady, we are not Sāmras; we are the guilds of the splendors of Dvārakā. //1//
Surely he has been propitiated by her and likewise by those of the past;
thus, in some ancient text, this distinction and generality are to be inferred. //2//
"Rukmiṇī is in Dvāravatī, while Rādhā is in the forest of Vṛndāvana.
Thus, her beloved is always the beloved; he shall be devoted to her alone and under her control. //3//
May that pair of paternal uncles, who have bestowed upon me an incomparable love for the truly devoted—a love that has become a tree within my heart—grant me their own final destination. (4)
May that pair of Lords, who bestow their own servitude, always be my refuge.

May that glorious Madhumardana, renowned for his auspiciousness and his beautiful form, who— having heard my cry from the banks of the Gaṅgā while I was in the waking state— again brought me from sleep into the supreme state of the three Vedas within the forest of Śrī Vṛndāvana; may he protect me.
I bow again and again to him, who possesses consciousness and who praises the lineage of the light. //6//
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇacaitanya, along with Sanātana and Rūpa; O Gopāla, O Raghunātha, O beloved of Vraja—protect me! //7//
Thus ends the poem named *Śrī-Saṅkalpa-druma*, which fulfills even my own desires— the abode of longing for the fullness of the forms of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa—
may everything belonging to me be offered at the feet of Śrī Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, this too would be exactly so. //8//
Thus ends the poem titled *Śrīsaṅkalpakalpadruma*.
